catalog_name: Clay Tablets and the Cyrus Cylinder
about: Writing began here, about 3200 BC in Uruk, Iraq: a reed pressed into wet clay to count grain and sheep. Left to right: the Flood Tablet, with a story of a great flood from the Epic of Gilgamesh (7th century BC); Plimpton 322, a table of right triangles (about 1800 BC); an accounting tablet from Uruk; a letter between kings from Amarna. Lying on its cradle is the Cyrus Cylinder (539 BC), a king's account of taking Babylon. Drawn here by hand from photographs and measurements: no free 3D scan of it exists.

Casts, oldest on the left. The Taung child (South Africa, about 2.8 million years). The Turkana boy, Homo erectus (Kenya, about 1.5 million years). A Neanderthal from La Ferrassie (France, about 50,000 years); Neanderthals buried their dead and lived alongside us. Cro-Magnon 1 (France, about 28,000 years): Homo sapiens, the only kind of human still alive. The bone that was found is brown. Drawn here by hand from photographs and measurements: no free 3D scan of it exists.

Namibia. This iron fell from space in prehistoric times. It formed 4.5 billion years ago in the core of a small planet that broke apart, so it is older than any rock on Earth. The pits on its skin melted as it fell through the air. On the cut face are crossing bands of nickel and iron that only grow in metal cooled over millions of years. Touch it: you are touching the inside of another world. Drawn here by hand from photographs and measurements: no free 3D scan of it exists.

Tanzania. The chopper on the right is about 1.8 million years old: a pebble with a few flakes knocked off to make an edge. The hand axe is about 1.2 million years old, flaked all over on both faces into a planned shape. Humans made this tool for over a million years, longer than anything else they have made. British Museum, London. Drawn here by hand from photographs and measurements: no free 3D scan of it exists.

catalog_name: Jade Burial Suit of Liu Sheng
about: China, 113 BC. Liu Sheng, a Han prince, was buried in a suit of 2,498 plates of jade sewn together with about 1.1 kg of gold wire. People believed jade kept a body from decay. It did not: when the tomb was opened in 1968, only the suit was left. Hebei Museum. Drawn here by hand from photographs and measurements: no free 3D scan of it exists.

Tanzania, 3.66 million years ago. Two early humans walked side by side across wet volcanic ash, which set hard like cement. These are the oldest footprints of upright walkers: a heel, an arch, and a big toe in line with the others. Found by Mary Leakey's team in 1978. The trail is 27 m long. This is a cast of part of it. Drawn here by hand from photographs and measurements: no free 3D scan of it exists.

Ethiopia, 3.2 million years ago. Found at Hadar in 1974 by Donald Johanson and Tom Gray: 40% of one skeleton of Australopithecus afarensis, about 1.1 m tall. Her knees and hips show she walked upright, on two legs, long before brains grew large. The bones that were found are brown; the pale ones are cast to fill the gaps. Named after a song played in camp that night. In Ethiopia she is Dinkinesh: you are marvellous. Drawn here by hand from photographs and measurements: no free 3D scan of it exists.

Thebes, Egypt, about 1000 BC. The coffin of a scribe at the great temple of Amun at Karnak. It is painted inside and out with gods, spells and the sky goddess Nut, whose wings fold over the chest. Its yellow varnish was meant to look like gold. Egyptians believed the coffin itself helped the dead pass into the next life. Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge. Drawn here by hand from photographs and measurements: no free 3D scan of it exists.

China, before 210 BC. Farmers digging a well near Xi'an in 1974 found an army of over 8,000 soldiers in clay, buried to guard Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of China, after his death. Each face is different. All were once painted, and the paint flakes away within minutes in the air. Here: an officer, two infantrymen and a kneeling archer. Their bronze weapons are gone. Drawn here by hand from photographs and measurements: no free 3D scan of it exists.

Greece, about 150 to 100 BC. In 1901 sponge divers found it in a shipwreck off the island of Antikythera. It is a hand-cranked computer of at least 30 bronze gears. It showed where the sun and moon would be on any day, the moon's phase, the coming eclipses and the dates of the Olympic Games. Nothing as complex was built again for over a thousand years. Beside the fragments is a working model of it. Athens. Drawn here by hand from photographs and measurements: no free 3D scan of it exists.

Congo, about 20,000 years old. A baboon's leg bone with rows of notches cut in groups, and a chip of quartz fixed in one end. One row reads 11, 13, 17, 19: the prime numbers between 10 and 20. Nobody knows if that was meant. It may be a tally, or a calendar of the moon. It is one of the oldest records of humans counting. Found in 1950; now in Brussels. Drawn six times bigger behind it. Drawn here by hand from photographs and measurements: no free 3D scan of it exists.

Egypt, 196 BC. One decree cut three times: in hieroglyphs for the gods, in Demotic for daily use, in Greek for the rulers. French soldiers found it at Rashid in 1799. Because the Greek could still be read, Champollion used it in 1822 to read hieroglyphs again after 1,400 years. This is how humans learned to read their own dead. British Museum, London. Drawn here by hand from photographs and measurements: no free 3D scan of it exists.

England, about AD 625. It was buried with a king, probably Raedwald of East Anglia, in a 27 m ship pulled up a hill and covered with earth. It was dug up in 1939 in hundreds of rusted pieces. This reconstruction shows how it shone: tinned bronze panels of dancing warriors, and a dragon flying up the face whose wings are the eyebrows. British Museum, London. Drawn here by hand from photographs and measurements: no free 3D scan of it exists.

Egypt, about 1323 BC. It lay on the face of the young king's mummy, inside three coffins in a tomb in the Valley of the Kings. Howard Carter found the tomb in 1922 and the mask in 1925. It is 10 kg of gold, inlaid with lapis lazuli, quartz, obsidian and coloured glass. Tutankhamun was about 19 when he died. Egyptians believed the face would help his spirit know its body. Cairo. Drawn here by hand from photographs and measurements: no free 3D scan of it exists.

Mammuthus primigenius. This is the real skeleton's shape: a 3D scan of the woolly mammoth at the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History, Washington (CC0), its bone coloured from photographs. About 3 m at the shoulder, with long curling tusks. Mammoths lived through the last ice age alongside humans, who hunted them, built huts of their bones and painted them on cave walls. The last ones died on Wrangel Island about 4,000 years ago, when the pyramids of Egypt were already old.
